whats-new-at-sheridan.title: What's New at Sheridan
whats-new-at-sheridan.lede: What's New at Sheridan brings every campus event from the SSU, Sheridan Clubs, Sheridan EDGE and Sheridan College into one consistent, filterable calendar, so Sheridan students can find an event that matters to them in seconds instead of checking four separate websites.

sections.title: Four websites, none of them have the full picture

blocks.text: How might we reduce the effort it takes for Sheridan students to discover campus events that are relevant to them?

Sheridan students who want to get involved on campus have to check multiple sites to find out what's going on at the SSU, Sheridan Clubs, Sheridan EDGE and Sheridan College. Each one has a different layout and none of them shows the full picture, so finding events takes time and it's easy to miss the ones that would have mattered.

sections.title: One place, one format, filtered your way

blocks.text: We saw an opportunity to bring these sources together. The site pulls live event data from each organizer through an API we built by scraping their event pages, displays everything in one consistent format, and presents it in a single place. Students can narrow events by date, campus, organizer and time of day, see what's on this week at a glance, and add events straight to their calendar.

Before designing anything, we mapped where each organizer published events and what kind of events they ran. Every source lived on a different platform, with its own layout and its own way of describing dates, places and times. There was no shared structure to build on, so we had to define one.

Whatever the source, every event is normalized into the same set of fields. This shared model is what makes the site feel like one calendar rather than four feeds stitched together, and it is what the filters and layouts are built on.

sections.title: Organized around the questions students ask

blocks.text: Students don't look for events by data source. They ask when, where and who. Each question became a facet that can be combined with the others, so "What's on this evening at Trafalgar?" is two clicks away.

items.name: When
items.question: What's on today? What about this week?

items.name: Who

sections.title: From a glance to the exact event

blocks.text: The page itself is ordered like an inverted pyramid. The most useful answer, how much is on this week, sits in the very first line, and each section below narrows from a broad overview to the specific event a student is looking for.

items.title: Navigation mirrors the facets
items.text: The main menu, This week · Organizers · Events · Campuses, maps directly to the ways students narrow events, so the menu doubles as a map of the content.

items.title: Every entry point lands on a filtered view
items.text: Choosing an organizer or campus anywhere on the page, including the footer, jumps to the event list with that filter already applied.

items.title: Plain, specific labels
items.text: "Evening (after 5 PM)" instead of a time code, and campus names paired with their city, so nobody has to guess what a label means.

items.title: Accessible by structure
items.text: A skip link straight to all events, colours checked against WCAG 2.2 AA, and event details that return focus where you left off.

blocks.text: Scrapers built with BeautifulSoup and Selenium collect events from each organizer's page, and a small API serves them in the shared format. The front end asks it for exactly the slice it needs, so every view and filter maps to a simple request.

sections.title: Where it could go from here

items.title: Test with students on every campus
items.text: Watch how students from Davis, Trafalgar and HMC actually search, and refine the facets and labels around it.

items.title: Automate the scraping
items.text: Run the scrapers on a schedule so new events show up, and changed or cancelled ones update, without anyone having to refresh the data by hand.

items.title: Remember a student's filters
items.text: Let students keep their campus and favourite organizers so the page opens on what matters to them.

items.title: Bring in more organizers
items.text: The shared content model means a new source only needs a scraper, not a redesign.

retro-radio-speaker.title: Retro Radio + Speaker
retro-radio-speaker.lede: Retro Radio + Speaker is an illustrated infographic that labels the main parts of the PRUNUS J-150, a vintage-style radio packed with modern features, and walks new owners through using it in five simple steps, so a glamper can get music or a station playing at camp without opening a manual.

highlights.label: steps from switched off to listening
listening modes: Bluetooth, FM, AM and SW
ways to power it: solar, battery and DC 5V

preview.label: Infographic
preview.alt: Infographic titled Retro Radio + Speaker. A line drawing of the PRUNUS J-150 radio labels eleven parts: antenna, handle, phone stand, solar panel, battery entrance, Bluetooth controls, ports, tuning knob, mode switch, on-off knob and speaker. Below it, five illustrated steps show how to turn it on, connect Bluetooth, switch to radio, tune a station and extend the antenna.

sections.title: Vintage on the outside, modern on the inside

blocks.text: The PRUNUS J-150 looks like an old-school transistor radio, with its wood-grain body and gold grille, but it hides modern features too: Bluetooth, a solar panel, a rechargeable battery, and USB and TF card playback. I chose it because I love how it mixes vintage style with new tech, and because there's a lot going on that isn't obvious at first glance.

My research centred on a persona who goes glamping: camping, with a few comforts brought along. For someone setting up a radio at a campsite, the features that matter most are the ones that work away from a wall outlet, so the solar panel, battery, Bluetooth and antenna all earn a clear place on the diagram.
The five steps were tested with new users and iterated on based on where they got stuck, so the final instructions reflect how first-time owners actually use the radio.

The infographic answers the two questions a new owner has, in the order they ask them: what am I looking at, and how do I use it? The layout follows the path a reader's eye already takes, from the title at the top left, to the labelled diagram, to a row of steps read left to right.

blocks.text: Each step zooms in on exactly the control it mentions, with one short instruction underneath, so the picture shows where and the words say what to do.

items.title: 1. Turn on
items.text: Turn the ON-OFF knob slightly to the right.

items.title: 2. Bluetooth
items.text: Slide the mode switch all the way to the left, then pair it with your phone or another device.

items.title: 3. Radio
items.text: Slide the mode switch to FM or AM.

items.title: 4. Tuning
items.text: Turn the tuning knob left and right until you find the station you want.

items.title: 5. Antenna
items.text: Extend the antenna for clearer radio audio.

sections.title: Line art with a little warmth

blocks.text: The radio is drawn in clean black line art so every control reads clearly, even in the small step close-ups. Soft peach and sage squares add warmth and a hint of the outdoors without competing with the labels.
